Title: Examining the effect of explanation on satisfaction and trust in AI diagnostic systems
Source Type: Journal Article (BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making)
Study Design & Methodology: Randomised controlled simulation experiments (Longitudinal tracking across three phases)
User Population: Laypeople (Undergraduate students acting as simulated patients)
Testing N: N = 193 (Across two experiments: N = 80 and N = 113)
AI Architecture: Simulated AI Chatbot (Scripted "MediBot.ai" Decision Tree)
Training N: Not applicable (Simulated system / Scripted decision tree)
Explanation Modality: Multimodal: Global Tutorials, Local Textual Rationales, Visual Probability Charts (LIME-inspired), and Case-Based Examples
Explanation Scope: Local & Global (Local: Specific GI diagnosis justifications; Global: General diagnostic process/tutorials)
Subjective Metrics: Post-interaction Likert scale adapted from the Explanation Satisfaction Scale (measuring satisfaction, trust, perceived accuracy, sufficiency, completeness, and usefulness). [Validated Psychometric Scales]
Objective Metrics: Not evaluated (System followed a scripted scenario rather than live algorithmic computation). [Not Evaluated]
Behavioural Metrics: Not evaluated. [Not Evaluated]
Quantitative Results: During an AI error (the re-diagnosis crisis), local explanations maintained significantly higher trust and satisfaction (P < 0.05). Global explanations failed entirely, crashing identically to the no-explanation control group.
Qualitative Insights: XAI is highly time-sensitive; patients only scrutinise explanations when the AI makes an error or uncertainty peaks. Multi-modal explanations (visuals and examples) act as critical shock absorbers, whereas text-only tutorials fail to protect trust during a crisis.
Key Findings (Concordance): The value of patient-facing XAI is highly temporal. Local, multi-modal explanations act as critical "shock absorbers" during algorithmic errors or re-diagnoses, preventing catastrophic drops in user trust that text-only rationales or global tutorials cannot mitigate.

Title: A Comprehensive Comparison and Evaluation of AI-Powered Healthcare Mobile Applications’ Usability
Study Design & Methodology: Observational usability evaluation
User Population: Laypeople (Aged 18-65 years, regular mHealth users without healthcare/tech backgrounds)
Testing N: N = 35 (Reported as 30 laypeople, 5 experts; objective data reflects subset of N = 12 laypeople)
AI Architecture: Opaque (Commercial Symptom Checker Apps)
Training N: Not reported (Evaluated commercial symptom checker apps)
Explanation Modality: Textual (Vague outputs lacking justifications or clinical links)
Explanation Scope: Local (Rationale for individual symptom triage outputs)
Delivery Format: Mobile Application (Commercial symptom checkers: Ada, Mediktor, WebMD)
Subjective Metrics: System Usability Scale (SUS) (0-100 scale, validated). [Validated Psychometric Scales]
Objective Metrics: Task success (0-1 scale), completion time (seconds), and error rates evaluated across 5 tasks. [Patient Comprehension & Accuracy]
Behavioural Metrics: Not evaluated (No longitudinal adherence tracking). [Not Evaluated]
Quantitative Results: System Usability Scale (SUS) scores favoured ADA (81.29) over Mediktor (76.51) and WebMD (70.61) (P < 0.001). However, ADA demonstrated the highest objective error rates and longest completion times (> 350 seconds) despite the highest satisfaction scores.
Qualitative Insights: Users struggled with vague outputs, noting that all apps failed custom XAI heuristics for explaining logic and proving reliability. Users explicitly requested logic summaries, progressive disclosure, and expanded language support.
Key Findings (Concordance): High perceived usability can mask objective danger. The "illusion of usability" means high subjective satisfaction scores do not equate to safe, understandable, or reliable AI logic.

Title: An adaptive machine learning framework integrating large language models to assess and enhance emotional intelligence in adolescents
Study Design & Methodology: Randomised controlled trial (Longitudinal dual-feedback adaptation)
User Population: Patients & Caregivers (Paediatric patients aged 3-16 years and their families)
AI Architecture: Stacked Ensemble ML + RAG (with Collaborative Filtering)
Training N: Not applicable (Ensemble model using dynamic web scraping and LLM)
Explanation Modality: Conversational Feature Attribution (SHAP values translated via LLM into natural language narratives)
Explanation Scope: Local (Highly individualised feedback tailored to specific neurocognitive profiles)
Subjective Metrics: Parental feedback collected longitudinally via an author-constructed, unvalidated 5-point Likert scale (parental satisfaction, perceived usefulness, trust, and activity rating) without a cited psychometric validation framework. [Unvalidated Questionnaires]
Objective Metrics: Pre- and post-intervention Emotional Intelligence (EI) scores measured via the validated Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ). [Patient Comprehension & Accuracy]
Behavioural Metrics: Completion rate (%) of recommended therapeutic activities. [Real-World Clinical]
Quantitative Results: The XAI group demonstrated massive clinical improvement in Emotional Intelligence (Cohen's d = 2.58) compared to the control group (d = 1.22). Qualitative Insights: Raw algorithmic transparency is useless to laypeople. LLM-generated narratives successfully translated mathematical SHAP values into family-friendly explanations, directly linking the AI's logic to the child's specific developmental needs and driving high parental trust.
Key Findings (Concordance): Translating mathematical feature importance into natural language narratives drastically improves parental trust, drives a 26% absolute increase in therapeutic adherence, and results in superior clinical outcomes compared to black-box recommendations.

Title: My diabetes care: an AI-based mobile app with conversational agent for type 2 diabetes selfmanagement

Qualitative Insights: Translating mathematical feature importance into natural language dialogue made neural network outcomes digestible for low-literacy populations. Users began to anthropomorphise the chatbot as they became comfortable with its interpretability.
Key Findings (Concordance): Integrating an explainable neural network with a natural language chatbot interface achieves high usability and clinical relevance, successfully resolving patient queries and driving improved self-management behaviours in resource-constrained settings.

Title:
Effects of explainable artificial intelligence in neurology
decision support
Source Type: Journal Article (Annals of Clinical and Translational Neurology)
Study Design & Methodology: Randomised controlled online experiment
User Population: Mixed (Laypeople and clinical neurology experts)
AI Architecture: Opaque (Random Forest Classifier) with Post-hoc XAI
Training N: N = 1,460 (Questions for DSS training and validation)
Explanation Modality: Feature Attribution (Comparison of SHAP and LIME algorithms)
Explanation Scope: Local (Rationale for specific clinical case predictions)
Subjective Metrics: Trust, perceived usefulness, and ease of use (7-point Likert scale adapted from the validated Technology Acceptance Model). [Validated Psychometric Scales]
Objective Metrics: Diagnostic accuracy (ability to select correct diagnosis/management plan pre- and post-AI recommendation). [Patient Comprehension & Accuracy]
Behavioural Metrics: Advice adherence (frequency of participants changing answers to match the AI, including incorrect advice). [Experimental Setting]
Quantitative Results: XAI did not significantly improve layperson diagnostic accuracy compared to the baseline (68% vs. 67%, P = 0.701). Laypeople were significantly more likely than experts to follow incorrect AI advice (P < 0.001) and reported significantly higher trust in the AI (P < 0.001).
Qualitative Insights: Laypeople exhibited blind trust in feature-based explanations (SHAP/LIME) because they appeared authoritative. Both lay and expert populations preferred logical, step-by-step decision trees over raw probability scores, which fail to explain the underlying reasoning.
Key Findings (Concordance): Post-hoc feature attributions create an illusion of understanding for laypeople, generating unwarranted trust and actively increasing adherence to incorrect AI advice because non-experts lack the domain knowledge to verify the logic.

Title: What Are the Users’ Needs? Design of a User-Centered Explainable Artificial Intelligence Diagnostic System
Country of Origin: China (Huazhong University of Science and Technology)
Source Type: Journal Article (International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction)
Study Design & Methodology: Mixed-methods human-computer interaction (HCI) evaluation (Two-phase design with focus groups and surveys)

AI Architecture: Simulated Machine Learning (Prototype UI testing 12 XAI components)
Training N: Not applicable (HCI prototype evaluation / Simulated system)
Explanation Modality: Hybrid Multi-Component Dashboard (12 graphical/textual configurations including counterfactuals, feature influence, and system performance)
Explanation Scope: Local & Global (Local: Patient-specific diagnoses and counterfactuals; Global: System performance and overarching rules)
Delivery Format: Slides and Paper Mock-ups (Dynamic system prototype)
Subjective Metrics: Explanation Satisfaction Scale (Hoffman et al., 2018) via 5-point Likert scale (evaluating system understanding, assessment of accuracy, usefulness to goal, and assessment of trust). [Validated Psychometric Scales]
Objective Metrics: Not evaluated (Human-Computer Interaction interface evaluation, not a test of algorithmic accuracy). [Not Evaluated]
Behavioural Metrics: Not evaluated. [Not Evaluated]
Quantitative Results: Diagnostic Recommendations (4.375/5.0) and Detailed Results (4.5/5.0) scored highest for usefulness and understanding. Counterfactual components scored the lowest (2.75/5.0).
Qualitative Insights: Standard clinician-centric XAI features (like counterfactuals and contradicting evidence) caused severe information overload and confusion in lay patients. Users also exhibited severe anxiety when shown raw algorithmic error rates, even if statistically low.
Key Findings (Concordance): Explainable AI design patterns developed for domain experts actively harm the lay user experience. Patient-facing XAI must avoid over-explanation (counterfactuals), prioritise actionable recommendations, and frame system accuracy using positive, anxiety-reducing language.

Title: Advancing Dermatological Diagnostics: Interpretable AI for Enhanced Skin Lesion Classification
Study Design & Methodology: Cross-sectional online survey evaluation
User Population: Mixed (73% laypeople; 27% dermatology experts)
AI Architecture: Opaque (ResNet-50 CNN) with Post-hoc ABELE Explainer
Training N: N = 25,331 (ISIC 2019 image dataset)
Explanation Modality: Hybrid: Visual Saliency Maps & Example-Based Synthetic Counterfactuals
Explanation Scope: Local (Image-specific predictions via latent space neighbourhoods)
Subjective Metrics: Confidence/Trust and perceived helpfulness of explanations (0-100 bespoke slider scales). [Unvalidated Questionnaires]
Objective Metrics: Diagnostic accuracy (success rate of categorising image classes). [AI Algorithm Performance]
Behavioural Metrics: Algorithm reliance/aversion (measured via change in user confidence after deliberate AI misclassification). [Experimental Setting]
Quantitative Results: Medical experts achieved 91.26% accuracy versus non-experts at 78.67%. Explanations increased overall confidence from 67.69% to 77.12%. During deliberate AI errors, expert confidence appropriately dropped by 14%, but non-expert confidence remained unchanged or paradoxically increased.
Qualitative Insights: Experts preferred technical detail (counter-exemplars), whereas laypeople experienced transparency overload. For older demographics (> 55 years), complex technical explanations increased scepticism rather than reducing it.
Key Findings (Concordance): Complex XAI designed for clinicians induces an "over-trust" phenomenon in laypeople (failing to trigger appropriate scepticism during errors) and backfires among older demographics, proving XAI must be health-literacy matched.

Title: Machine learning-based prediction models in medical decision-making in kidney disease: patient, caregiver, and clinician perspectives on trust and appropriate use

Source Type: Journal Article (Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association)

Explanation Scope: Local & Global (Local: Individual patient application; Global: Population-level training data/model metrics)

Key Findings (Concordance): Dialysis stakeholders accept ML mortality predictions provided they meet an 80% accuracy threshold and incorporate SDOH. However, ethical implementation mandates a "human-in-the-loop" to act as an empathy buffer and the preservation of patient autonomy to opt out.

Title: Exploring and Promoting Diagnostic Transparency and Explainability in Online Symptom Checkers
Source Type: Conference Proceeding (CHI '21 - ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
Study Design & Methodology: Mixed-methods study (Formative qualitative interviews followed by a randomised Latin-square lab experiment with role-play scenarios)
User Population: Laypeople (General healthcare consumers)
AI Architecture: Transparent / Rule-based Expert System (Dialogflow + Clinical Decision Tree)
Training N: Not applicable (Rule-based decision tree without ML training)
Explanation Modality: Conversational XAI (Comparison of In-Line Rationales, Post-Hoc Feature Summaries, and Post-Hoc Case Examples)
Explanation Scope: Local (Triage outcome rationale based on individual symptom inputs)
Subjective Metrics: Post-task 7-point Likert scale evaluating 8 constructs (quality, control, effectiveness, trust, transparency, satisfaction, awareness, learning) and cognitive load via the NASA-TLX index. [Validated Psychometric Scales]
Objective Metrics: Task completion time (latency measured in minutes). [Patient Comprehension & Accuracy]
Behavioural Metrics: Scenario-based simulated medical decision-making (assessing appropriate triage behaviour). [Experimental Setting]
Quantitative Results: XAI significantly boosted transparency and trust compared to the baseline (P < 0.001). Only post-hoc explanation models significantly improved perceived diagnostic quality (P < 0.05). XAI did not increase cognitive load.
Qualitative Insights: Lay users strongly prefer post-hoc explanations, as step-by-step in-line rationales interrupt conversational flow. Anchoring XAI to authoritative sources (e.g., the CDC) and phrasing explanations as actionable scripts act as powerful catalysts for trust.
Key Findings (Concordance): Augmenting symptom checkers with XAI significantly improves trust without increasing cognitive load. Crucially, lay users prefer post-hoc summaries over step-by-step in-line rationales, especially when explanations are anchored to recognisable authoritative medical sources.

Title:
The Influence of Explainable Artificial Intelligence and Mental
Health Literacy on Professional Psychological Help-Seeking
Behavior: The Mediating Role of Psychological
Problem Cognition
Study Design & Methodology: Randomised controlled online experiment
User Population: Laypeople (General population with baseline mental health and AI attitude controls)
Testing N: N = 346 (Across two experiments: N = 168 and N = 178)
AI Architecture: Simulated LLM (ChatGPT-4.0 mock interface)
Training N: Not applicable (Simulated interface via pre-trained GPT-4.0)
Explanation Modality: Structured Textual (Susceptibility, Severity, Effectiveness, and Accessibility dimensions)
Explanation Scope: Local (Rationale for specific, individualised symptom inputs)
Subjective Metrics: Perceived explainability (3-item scale), psychological problem cognition (14-item scale), mental health literacy (22-item MHLS), attitudes toward AI (4-item AIAS-4), and help-seeking intention. [Validated Psychometric Scales]
Objective Metrics: Not evaluated. [Not Evaluated]
Behavioural Metrics: Professional psychological help-seeking behaviour (measured via a 4-stage simulated appointment booking task scoring milestone completion). [Experimental Setting]
Quantitative Results: XAI significantly increased help-seeking behaviour scores (P = 0.002). For low mental health literacy users, the behavioural increase was massive (P < 0.001); for high literacy users, there was no significant difference between the XAI and control conditions (P = 0.719).
Qualitative Insights: XAI acts as a cognitive mediator, shifting internal problem recognition and reducing the psychological resistance associated with black-box models. Users prioritised information regarding severity and accessibility over simple diagnostic labels.
Key Findings (Concordance): XAI functions as a critical "knowledge equaliser." It significantly enhances trust and drives tangible behavioural compliance for low-literacy users, but offers marginal benefits for those with high baseline health literacy due to a ceiling effect.

Title: Incorporating end-user perspectives into the development of a machine learning algorithm for first time perinatal depression prediction

Explanation Scope: Global (Population-level causal pathways predicting depression)

Title: The Impact of Explanations on Layperson Trust in Artificial Intelligence–Driven Symptom Checker Apps:Experimental Study
Source Type: Journal Article (Journal of Medical Internet Research)
Study Design & Methodology: Randomised controlled online experiment
Clinical Domain: Primary Care (Migraine vs. Temporal Arteritis Triage)
User Population: Laypeople (Healthy adults from the general population)
AI Architecture: Simulated Opaque Model (Evaluating Post-hoc Explanations)
Training N: Not applicable (Simulated system / Scripted video prototype)
Explanation Modality: Textual (Comparison of Input Influence, Social Proof, and Counterfactual Explanations)
Explanation Scope: Local (Rationale for individual diagnostic outputs)
Subjective Metrics: Multi-dimensional Trust scale (12-item survey evaluating faith, comprehension, and depth; adapted from Hoffman's Scale). [Validated Psychometric Scales]
Objective Metrics: Not evaluated. [Not Evaluated]
Behavioural Metrics: Self-reported behavioural intention (inclination to use and propensity to follow advice). [Experimental Setting]
Quantitative Results: Explanation modality showed no significant effect on trust for common diseases (P = 0.65) but demonstrated marginal significance for rare diseases (P = 0.09). Qualitative Insights: Laypeople lack the medical knowledge to evaluate algorithmic mechanisms, often interpreting explanations as clustering cues. Users exhibited causal discounting if the AI did not explicitly rule out the alternative severe disease (the "foil") they were most worried about.
Key Findings (Concordance): XAI trust is highly context-dependent. For lay populations, XAI can dangerously increase surface-level trust without improving true comprehension, especially if the explanation fails to address the patient's pre-existing health anxieties.

Title: ChatMyopia: An AI agent for myopia-related consultation in primary eye care settings
Study Design & Methodology: Randomised controlled trial (Prospective waiting-room intervention)
User Population: Patients (Aged 18-60 years, seeking myopia consultations)
AI Architecture: Modular Multi-modal LLM (Mistral-123B + Vision Transformer + Clinical RAG)
Training N: N = 2,769 (Fundus images for Vision Transformer training)
Explanation Modality: Hybrid: Textual (Evidence Traceability) & Visual Saliency Heatmaps
Explanation Scope: Local (Evidence-backed interpretation of individual patient fundus imagery)
Delivery Format: Tablet-based Application (Interactive session deployed in clinical waiting room)
Subjective Metrics: Patient satisfaction measured via the validated Medical Interview Satisfaction Scale-Revised (C-MISS-R), a 7-aspect perception scale, and the Decision Conflict Scale (DCS-10). [Validated Psychometric Scales]
Objective Metrics: Algorithmic performance (accuracy, AUROC, sensitivity, specificity) and expert-evaluated metrics (blinded specialists rating AI utility, relevance, and safety). [AI Algorithm Performance]
Behavioural Metrics: Not evaluated. [Not Evaluated]
Quantitative Results: The XAI group reported significantly higher overall satisfaction (P = 0.018) and cognitive understanding (P = 0.013). Qualitative Insights: Traceable interpretability (RAG) allowed patients to verify clinical support, facilitating error identification. The interactive, empathetic waiting-room intervention successfully bridged the information gap prior to face-to-face consultations.
Key Findings (Concordance): Deploying an interactive, explainable LLM agent in the waiting room significantly increases patient satisfaction, disease self-awareness, and clinical safety, proving to be a measurably superior supplement to traditional printed educational materials.

Title: Effect of AI Explanations on Human Perceptions of Patient-Facing AI-Powered Healthcare Systems
Country of Origin: USA (Pace University, IBM Research, University of Illinois)
Study Design & Methodology: Randomised 2x2 factorial online experiment (Testing transparency levels and model performance)
User Population: Laypeople (General healthcare consumers)
AI Architecture: Transparent / Support Vector Machines (Linear Kernels + TF-IDF)
Training N: N = 727 (Crowd-annotated radiology sentences for training)
Explanation Modality: Textual Saliency (Feature Highlighting of predictive keywords)
Explanation Scope: Local & Global (Local: Sentence-level rationales in radiology reports; Global: Overall model accuracy metrics)
Subjective Metrics: User perception measured via a 5-point Likert scale (adapted from TAM) assessing perceived usefulness, sufficiency of information, understandability, and trustworthiness. [Validated Psychometric Scales]
Objective Metrics: Algorithmic performance (mathematical accuracy of the underlying SVM models against expert gold standard). [AI Algorithm Performance]
Behavioural Metrics: Human-AI agreement (tracking whether users aligned their final diagnostic decision with the AI or actively rejected it). [Experimental Setting]
Quantitative Results: High transparency significantly increased perceived understanding (P < 0.001) but had no main effect on overall trust. When the underlying AI model was weak, providing explanations actively decreased user trust (P = 0.04).
Qualitative Insights: Model accuracy is the absolute strongest driver of trust. XAI triggers algorithm aversion when the model is weak, as highlighting incorrect features explicitly exposes the system's flaws to the user.
Key Findings (Concordance): The "XAI backfire effect" proves that transparency does not inherently build trust for laypeople. High algorithmic accuracy is an absolute prerequisite; explaining a weak or incorrect model actively erodes user trust and perceived usefulness compared to a black box.
